title: Chat onramp — stability, debugging, and fallback patterns
summary: Intro demo of Redwood hosted chat/text generation. Covered streaming modes, key parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), retry/idempotency strategies, and console debugging tools. Customer concerned about latency spikes, data residency, and audit logs; discussed Dedicated vs Hosted tradeoffs and Optimize recommendations (batching/prefix cache). Agreed next steps: SE-run latency benchmark, share SSO & SOC2 docs, follow-up pilot proposal.
action_items: Marcus Chen — run 3-tier latency benchmark with Velaris sample payloads by 2025-06-12
Lena Ortiz — send SOC2 and SSO integration doc by 2025-06-06
Aaron Kim (Velaris) — provide a 1-week sample traffic trace by 2025-06-09
next_steps: Share pilot pricing and Dedicated capacity note
Grant Velaris sandbox access + demo credentials
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-06-05 15:30 PDT / Duration: 42 min / Attendees: Lena Ortiz (Redwood AE), Marcus Chen (Redwood SE), Ibrahim Malik (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (CTO, Velaris), Evan Murphy (Sr BE), Sandra Lopez (PM), Aaron Kim (DevOps)

Summary auto-note: quick hosted chat onramp walkthrough focused on robustness and debugging; live demo of streaming, retry and console traces; action items agreed.

00:00 Lena Ortiz: okay hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm lena with redwood inference, excited to run through a short onramp and show how streaming + retries work, we have marcus and ibrahim from se side as well, thanks for taking the time

00:12 Priya Singh: thanks lena yeah we are short on time so if you can focus on latency edges and operational debugging that'd be great, our primary concern is spikes during business hours, and also audit logging for compliance

00:23 Marcus Chen: absolutely, quick outline — i'll demo a hosted chat endpoint, show streaming vs sync, tweak params (temperature, top_p, max_tokens), then show retry behavior and console trace artifacts; then we'll talk about caching and batching suggestions from optimize

00:37 Evan Murphy: quick Q — do you all use SSE or http2 for streaming? we've had mixed results with client libraries

00:43 Marcus Chen: good question — our hosted streams use chunked transfer over HTTP/1.1 by default and also support http2 streams in some SDKs; SSE and websocket clients are patterns we see in the field — the important bit is idempotency and resume semantics which i'll show

01:05 Sandra Lopez: and what about chunk sizes? sometimes we see microburst token floods that blow up latency

01:12 Ibrahim Malik: right, we expose streaming chunks at token-granularity but the runtime applies micro-batching under the hood; you can tune the max_buffer_ms and batch_window to smooth bursts, or enable prefix cache so common prefixes return from cache and reduce token generation overhead

01:35 Lena Ortiz: i'm going to share the console, you should see the trace on your side, let me know if anything is blocked

01:42 (screen share starts)

02:00 Marcus Chen: here's a test chat session — request comes in, we start SSE chunks, you can see request id ff-9812 in the header. I'm going to set temperature to 0.2 and max_tokens to 120 to favour deterministic short replies

02:18 Evan Murphy: can you show a higher temperature to see stochastic behavior? our product sometimes needs creative variants

02:24 Marcus Chen: sure — switching to 0.8 now. note: when you increase temperature and top_p you increase variance and occasionally token-latency due to sampling paths — cost and latency tradeoffs

03:10 Priya Singh: tolerance question — what are SLOs on p95 latency on hosted? we need to promise 300ms for short prompts in the US region

03:18 Ibrahim Malik: our public SLO is 99th percentile within X ms depending on model class; for short prompts and smaller models p95 can be under 300ms in our hosted clusters — but we recommend a smoke benchmark with your prompt distribution; that's one of the action items

03:45 Marcus Chen: i'm going to intentionally interrupt the stream to demo retry behavior — simulate a connection drop mid-response. you should see partial tokens and then a resumed request with same id and idempotency key

04:05 (simulated disconnect)

04:12 Sandra Lopez: saw it, the client reconnected and resumed but there was a small duplicate fragment — is dedup handled server side?

04:20 Marcus Chen: good catch. we de-duplicate by (request_id + sequence_number) if you pass an idempotency key we will ensure we don't double-count tokens for billing or stateful ops; for streaming fragments the client is recommended to stitch chunks on rejoin using sequence markers

04:46 Aaron Kim: on billing — if a stream restarts mid-token do you bill the partial token twice? that was a pain with our previous vendor

04:55 Marcus Chen: we bill by token completed on the runtime; partial fragments are not double-billed when you use the idempotency key and resume semantics; offline logs show the handshake and final token count

05:23 Lena Ortiz: switching gears — console traces. You can see a trace view per request with timeline: routing, kernel selection, batching wait, runtime exec, and KV cache hit/miss. I'll open an example trace that shows a KV cache hit

05:50 (console demo navigates to traces)

06:02 Marcus Chen: here — KV cache hit for a common system prompt — that cut the generation latency by about 30% in this sample. optimize will suggest cache candidates based on frequent prefix fingerprints

06:30 Priya Singh: hmm interesting. what about PII in prompts — if we cache prefixes are we storing sensitive text in cache? compliance team will ask

06:39 Ibrahim Malik: good point — KV/prefix cache can be configured to exclude sensitive inputs, or to encrypt cache keys and set TTLs. For regulated workloads we recommend Private deployment or Dedicated with customer-managed KMS so you control cache encryption and retention policies

07:05 Evan Murphy: can you show a failure where batching delays cause latency spikes? we'd like to understand the failure mode

07:13 Marcus Chen: yes — i'm going to increase batch_window to 200ms and show what happens under light traffic — you can see that introductory latency jumps because the runtime waits to accumulate the batch; under steady traffic this improves throughput and lowers per-token cost, but under bursty light traffic it can hurt p95

07:49 Sandra Lopez: so what's the recommended pattern for our use case — interactive chat with sporadic peaks at 10–20 qps?

07:58 Ibrahim Malik: start with conservative batch_window (20–50ms) and enable autoscaling with burst capacity; enable prefix cache for common system messages; use adaptive batching which reduces the window on low QPS; Optimize will produce a tailored config once we ingest your traffic trace

08:30 Priya Singh: can you walk through retry backoff policy — we have a client library that simple-retries with fixed backoff and that created thundering sometimes

08:40 Marcus Chen: we recommend exponential backoff with jitter and an idempotency key; on 5xx errors prefer a longer backoff and fallback to a cheaper model variant if the primary model is overloaded. Redwood's SDK supports automatic retry hooks and the console surfaces retry counts per route

09:12 Evan Murphy: fallback to cheaper model — is that an automatic policy or something we have to wire? we'd like graceful degradation to cheaper but still acceptable output quality

09:19 Ibrahim Malik: you can set routing policies: preferred model -> fallbacks list -> region fallback. The platform can auto-fallback based on capacity thresholds you define. We also support canary rollouts and gradual traffic shifting so you can test fallback quality with a small percent of requests

09:52 Lena Ortiz: i'm going to demo a simulated overload where auto-fallback kicks in to a quantized model variant — watch the quality diff and cost delta in the console metrics

10:10 (demo: simulated overload)

10:25 Marcus Chen: console metrics show throughput spike, fallback triggered to quantized-4bit variant, latency stayed within SLO but output brevity changed slightly; you can set a quality budget so some routes never fallback if you need hard guarantees

10:55 Sandra Lopez: how do we validate quality regressions? we run a few key prompts, we need alerting on regressions post-deploy

11:03 Ibrahim Malik: Optimize integrates with evals — you can pin prompt suites and get quality regression alerts tied to rollout events. We can also run A/B evals as part of canary rollouts and failback automatically if quality drops below a threshold

11:34 Priya Singh: on security — SOC2, audit logs, SSO — can you send the docs? also need retention options for logs and transcripts

11:42 Lena Ortiz: yes i'll share SOC2 and SSO guide after the call. retention and log export can be set per-tenant; Dedicated or Private gives you more retention control and on-prem audit streams

12:01 Evan Murphy: curious about developer ergonomics — how do we debug in staging? can we replay a request from the console?

12:09 Marcus Chen: you can replay a trace from the console to reproduce; traces include full request metadata (not PII unless you capture it) and you can replay to a sandbox model. We also surface kernel selections and batch composition so you can see why a particular request waited in a batch

12:40 Sandra Lopez: any gotchas with idempotency keys and streaming where clients generate new keys on reconnect? that broke our stitching logic before

12:48 Marcus Chen: we recommend clients generate a stable idempotency key per logical user-turn, not per TCP connection. On reconnect the client should reuse the same key and pass the last-seen sequence number to resume. We'll send a short best-practices note for streaming SDK usage

13:12 Priya Singh: demo request — can you run a quick benchmark with our sample prompts and show p95 numbers? we'll want that before committing to a pilot

13:20 Marcus Chen: yes that's part of the SE action item — we'll run three traffic shapes (low QPS bursty, steady medium, high sustained) and return p50/p95/p99 and cost estimates

13:40 Aaron Kim: about networking — any special egress whitelisting or VPC peering needed for hosted? we have strict outbound rules

13:47 Ibrahim Malik: hosted requires outbound to our API endpoints; for stricter networking we can do Dedicated with private egress or Private deployment with VPC peering; we'll include details in the doc pack we send

14:10 Lena Ortiz: want to quickly show the SDK snippet for streaming resume and idempotency — i'll paste a node snippet

14:18 (code snippet shared)

14:25 Marcus Chen: snippet highlights: set idempotencyKey = userTurnId, pass lastSequence when reconnecting, handle partial event types (start, token, end, error). Use backoff with jitter on error codes 429 and 5xx

14:50 Evan Murphy: sometimes our front-end throttles erroneously and we see 429s at low traffic — how do you recommend throttling/queueing on client side?

14:58 Marcus Chen: implement client-side token bucket with burst allowance and fallback UI; server side has rate limits per API key and per route, and console will surface throttle panels; for graceful UX respond with cached content or short canned fallback during throttling windows

15:25 Sandra Lopez: are there any costs to enabling tracing and debugging in the console? we worry about storage egress charges

15:33 Lena Ortiz: trace retention is configurable; for extended retention there's a small add-on and you can export to your own S3 for long-term archive to avoid egress surprises

15:55 Priya Singh: okay this was helpful. to recap — se will run benchmarks, lena sends security and onboarding docs, velaris will provide sample traces and timetable; pilot proposal after benchmark

16:12 (wrap up)

End of transcript: actual call ended at ~16:12 PDT.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlaps and a few proper nouns may be mis-transcribed (model names, kernel flags).
